longForm.title: The Siege of Khe Sanh, 1968: Terrain, Attrition, and the Dien Bien Phu Question
longForm.excerpt: For 77 days beginning 21 January 1968, PAVN forces encircled 6,000 US Marines at Khe Sanh Combat Base. Westmoreland compared it to Dien Bien Phu. The comparison was wrong in ways that mattered operationally — and the PAVN may have intended it to be.
paragraphs: Khe Sanh Combat Base sat on a plateau at approximately 485 meters elevation in Quang Tri Province, nine kilometers from the Laotian border and 25 kilometers south of the DMZ. The base controlled Route 9, the only improved road running west toward Laos, and sat within the ring of hills — 861, 881 North, 881 South, 950, 1015 — that dominated the surrounding terrain. Whoever held those hills could observe and engage the base. Whoever held the base could threaten PAVN infiltration routes through the DMZ corridor. The Marines had been at Khe Sanh since 1962 in various forms. By January 1968, the 26th Marine Regiment, under Colonel David Lownds, held the base with approximately 6,000 Marines and 500 ARVN Rangers. PAVN intelligence placed two divisions — the 304th and the 325C — in the surrounding hills, totaling an estimated 20,000 to 40,000 troops. The ground situation was clear. The question was what the PAVN intended to do with it.

The answer to that question was never definitively established, which is part of what makes Khe Sanh operationally interesting. General Vo Nguyen Giap later denied that Khe Sanh was intended as the primary effort. American commanders at the time, including Westmoreland, believed it was — believed that the PAVN intended to overrun the base and create a Dien Bien Phu-style propaganda victory, and structured their response accordingly. Westmoreland moved substantial US combat power to I Corps, reinforced Khe Sanh by airlift, and requested contingency planning for tactical nuclear weapons use if the base appeared in danger of falling. Whether the PAVN siege was a genuine attempt to take the base or a strategic deception designed to fix US attention on Khe Sanh while the Tet Offensive's urban attacks were prepared remains a genuine historical question. The documentary record from Hanoi has not resolved it.

The hilltop outposts were tactically critical and the first targets of the siege. On the night of 20-21 January 1968, PAVN forces attacked Hill 861. The Marines at 861 held, but the attack confirmed what signals intelligence had been suggesting: the siege was beginning. On 21 January, PAVN artillery and rocket fire struck the base itself, detonating the main ammunition dump and destroying 1,500 tons of munitions. The base's runway was damaged. The communications infrastructure took hits. Lownds had been preparing for this; his defensive plans included the outlying hill positions as integral parts of the perimeter rather than detached outposts, a lesson drawn directly from the French experience at Dien Bien Phu where isolated hilltop positions had been taken sequentially.

The critical operational difference from Dien Bien Phu was airpower. At Dien Bien Phu in 1954, the French air assets were inadequate and the Viet Minh's antiaircraft suppressed the resupply airdrops that the garrison depended on. At Khe Sanh in 1968, the United States had overwhelming air superiority and the organizational infrastructure to apply it continuously. Operation Niagara — the air support campaign for Khe Sanh — delivered more than 100,000 tactical air sorties and 2,700 B-52 Arc Light strikes around the base perimeter during the 77-day siege. The tonnage of ordnance dropped in the Khe Sanh area during January-April 1968 exceeded the total Allied bombing of Japan in 1944. The PAVN units in the hills absorbed this continuously. Their ability to do so, while sustaining the siege, was itself an operational achievement that received less attention than the Marine defenders.

Resupply was the central tactical problem of the siege. The runway at Khe Sanh could be used under fire, but not reliably, and large transport aircraft were vulnerable to PAVN antiaircraft fire during approach and landing. The Marine Corps and Air Force developed the Low Altitude Parachute Extraction System (LAPES) for delivering heavy cargo without landing, with aircraft skimming the runway at low altitude and deploying parachutes to drag pallets out the rear. The system worked but was imprecise. The C-123 and C-130 crews who flew resupply missions into Khe Sanh under fire were doing so with full knowledge of the ground threat; several aircraft were hit on approach, and one C-123 was shot down on 6 February, killing 43 people. The helicopter crews of Marine Medium Helicopter Squadron 361 flew resupply to the outlying hill positions throughout the siege, often in weather and under fire simultaneously.

The PAVN ground assault that Westmoreland feared never came — not against the main base. The attacks on the outlying positions were costly and repeated: Hill 861A was attacked on 5 February by elements of the 325C Division, and the fighting was close enough that Marines used pistols and entrenching tools before the position was secured. The Special Forces camp at Lang Vei, southwest of Khe Sanh, was overrun on 7 February by PAVN forces using Soviet PT-76 amphibious tanks — the first use of armor against US forces in Vietnam. The Khe Sanh base itself, despite continuous artillery, mortar, and rocket bombardment that damaged nearly every structure above ground and forced the garrison into underground bunkers for much of the siege, was never subjected to a coordinated infantry assault in the manner of Dien Bien Phu. The reasons the PAVN withheld that assault — whether because the air campaign made it prohibitively costly, because the strategic situation changed with Tet, or because it was never intended — are not established in the available record.

Operation Pegasus, the ground relief of Khe Sanh, began on 1 April 1968 with elements of the 1st Cavalry Division airmobiling into positions along Route 9 and the 3rd Marines attacking west overland. The route was cleared and ground contact with the base established on 8 April. The PAVN forces that had surrounded Khe Sanh withdrew in good order. US casualties during the siege totaled 274 killed and 2,541 wounded at the base itself, with additional casualties at the outlying positions. PAVN losses are estimated at between 10,000 and 15,000, primarily from the air campaign, though the methodology for estimating enemy dead around Khe Sanh was the body count, which had the reliability problems it had everywhere else in the war.

Westmoreland's decision to hold Khe Sanh, and his subsequent claim that it was a major American victory, has been contested. The base was abandoned by the Marines in June 1968 — two months after its relief — when MACV determined that its operational value did not justify the cost of garrisoning it. The abandonment was not announced in advance. The PAVN reoccupied the position after the Marines departed. Critics argued that Khe Sanh had fixed US strategic attention and diverted resources while the real PAVN effort — Tet — succeeded in its political objective of demonstrating that the war was not nearly as won as the Johnson administration had been claiming. Defenders of the decision argued that Khe Sanh had inflicted disproportionate casualties on the PAVN and had protected the northern I Corps from a conventional PAVN thrust. Both arguments have documentary support. The question of which was the primary PAVN intention at Khe Sanh remains open.

shortForm.title: Operation Niagara: The Air Campaign That Kept Khe Sanh Alive
shortForm.excerpt: Operation Niagara delivered over 100,000 tactical sorties and 2,700 B-52 strikes around Khe Sanh's perimeter during the 77-day siege. It was the most concentrated application of airpower in support of a single ground position in the history of warfare. It worked — and its success concealed how close the situation had come.
paragraphs: Operation Niagara was planned before the siege began. General Momyer, commanding Seventh Air Force, understood from the beginning of the PAVN buildup around Khe Sanh that the base could not be held by ground forces alone — the garrison of 6,000 could not repel 20,000 or more PAVN regulars in a conventional assault without continuous close air support. The planning problem was target acquisition: PAVN forces in the hills around Khe Sanh were dug in, camouflaged, and operating at night. The solution was a sensor network — ADSID acoustic sensors airdropped into the jungle that detected movement and transmitted to an analysis center at Infiltration Surveillance Center Nakhon Phanom in Thailand. The sensor data gave strike planners an approximate picture of PAVN positions and movement patterns. It was approximate, not precise. The B-52 Arc Light strikes that hit the ridgelines around Khe Sanh were planned to saturate grid squares rather than strike point targets.

The volume of ordnance was unprecedented. During the 77-day siege, aircraft flying Niagara missions dropped approximately 96,000 tons of ordnance on the Khe Sanh area — more than the total tonnage dropped on Japan in 1944. The B-52 strikes were particularly consequential; the 750-pound bombs from a three-aircraft cell could strip the vegetation from a ridgeline and destroy fortifications that would have survived artillery. PAVN soldiers who survived the Arc Light strikes and were subsequently captured described the psychological and physical effects in terms that matched earlier accounts from German soldiers who had experienced Allied strategic bombing: the concussion alone was disorienting at considerable distances from the detonation point. The PAVN units maintained their siege positions despite this. Their ability to sustain combat effectiveness under continuous air attack for 77 days was an organizational and material achievement that American operational assessments tended to undercount.

The cost of Niagara was real. The aircrew casualties were not insignificant, and the logistics of sustaining that sortie rate for nearly three months strained Air Force and Navy maintenance capacity. But the calculation was sound: without Niagara, Khe Sanh would not have held. The French at Dien Bien Phu had faced a siege by a force with comparable numbers under comparable terrain conditions, without comparable air support. The French garrison fell in 55 days. The Marines held for 77. The difference was not the quality of the defenders — it was the air campaign. What Niagara could not resolve was the larger strategic question: whether holding Khe Sanh at this cost, in this location, for these reasons, was a rational allocation of the most powerful tactical air fleet in the world.

onThisDay.headline: HMS Sheffield Hit by Argentine Exocet Missile During the Falklands War
onThisDay.summary: On 4 May 1982, the British Type 42 destroyer HMS Sheffield was struck by an AM39 Exocet air-launched missile fired by an Argentine Super Étendard aircraft during the Falklands War. The missile did not detonate but its unburned rocket fuel started a fire that could not be controlled; 20 sailors were killed and the ship was abandoned. Sheffield sank under tow on 10 May. It was the first Royal Navy vessel lost in combat since the Second World War.
